doc.title: Al Vollmer interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Hartford, New York, June 8, 2017

title: Prejudice against jazz at Hamilton
summary: Jazz was not accepted at Hamilton in 1948-52; a professor misread his blues noodling, and Vollmer reflects on 'serious music' language.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: Okay. I’m going to flip back to Hamilton for a minute and then we’ll come back to that. Because I was curious, you were at Hamilton from —
’48 to ’52. Was there a division in things that people wanted to listen to? You liked Jelly Roll Morton —

Well jazz wasn’t accepted at Hamilton then, no. Because I remember I had learned some blues chords and I was playing them in Silliman Hall, and one of the — which was the music department at the time. And one of the professors looked in and I had to tell him what I was doing wasn’t jazz, I mean I was just noodling on the piano. Well because — he said — he almost felt like, you know, that he couldn’t perceive what was jazz because maybe nobody was telling him. Or anyway, well I think there was a prejudice against jazz by the older generation. There just was. Because we had it in the language. And the language is very important. We call classical music “serious music.” And therefore, semantically, pop music or jazz music or whatever you know, it happens to be, what the people come up with, is then frivolous.
